awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Eco-engineered System for Coastal Protection
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impact of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is in providing clear and measurable environmental benefits by restoring shorelines, enhancing benthic infauna, seagrass habitats, and federally protected mangrove areas. By potentially reducing wave energy by up to 70%, mitigating erosion and flood risks, it would protect local communities and could become the preferred first line of defense against beach erosion and marine life habitat destruction in the nation. The company’s proprietary honeycomb reef arch structures would allow for beach restoration in previously inaccessible areas including military bases, shallow water zones, areas far from staging sites, and more. Historically, riprap (layer of large boulders installed on the shoreline) has been the go-to solution wave attenuation, but its installation cost alone is quite high. In contrast, the installation cost of the proposed technology is estimated to be 10X lower and thus this technology provides a compelling value proposition. Since the annual coastal property loss caused by beach erosion is around $500M in the U.S., there is significant commercial potential for the proposed technology. The project is in alignment with National Science Foundation’s key priority of natural disaster prevention or mitigation.


The intellectual merit of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project lies in the iterative development of material of construction for the company’s bio-inspired, large-scale, modular, stackable honeycombs units, called Reef Arches, a nature-based solution deployed on coastline for wave attenuation, shore protection and marine life restoration. Inshore oysters’ reefs are proven to be effective methods of wave attenuation & oysters prefer calcium-rich substrate to grow. The final material composition of the proposed honeycomb arches must be such that the arches can function on many fronts: they must integrate seamlessly with the company’s manufacturing process to maintain the mold’s integrity over thousands of production cycles, support sensitive marine life- such as coral and oysters- without harming local aquatic ecosystems, withstand relentless marine forces exerted by waves, currents, and biofouling, and stay within local regulatory constraints. They should also be compatible with the company’s breakthrough method of installation, one that does not use any heavy machinery, without breakage during the process. Phase I R&D thus will involve materials development to meet a complex set of requirements – mechanical, chemical, biological, legal, and logistical to find a balance that enables large scale production and installation of honeycomb reef arches for coastline resilience.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Reef Arches develops eco-engineered honeycomb structures made from marine-compatible concrete that are deployed along coastlines to protect shorelines, reduce erosion, and create thriving habitat for coral, oysters, and other marine life. Unlike traditional hard armoring such as seawalls and rock revetments, Reef Arches work with natural coastal processes rather than against them — trapping sediment, reducing wave energy, and providing complex three-dimensional surfaces that marine organisms rapidly colonize. Prior to this award, the company had promising prototypes and early field data showing wave energy reductions of 37 to 54 percent and more than 11 inches of sediment buildup behind deployed units. However, the company lacked the manufacturing processes and deployment methods needed to produce and install these structures at commercial scale. This Phase I award funded the research needed to close that gap.

During the award period, the team conducted extensive testing to identify the best concrete materials, mold designs, and production procedures for large-scale manufacturing. A specialized concrete formulation was identified that sets rapidly, achieves high strength, maintains a neutral acidity level ideal for marine life, and can be produced at a rate of up to six units per day — compared to just one unit per day with conventional concrete. The team developed a systematic method for determining the precise moment at which freshly cast units can be safely removed from their molds, based on monitoring internal concrete temperature during curing. This discovery significantly reduces production time and defects. Testing also showed that optimizing the size and proportion of sand and gravel in the concrete mix reduced cement consumption by approximately 25 percent, lowering production costs. Multiple mold systems were developed and tested, including resin-based molds suitable for spray production and precision metal molds designed for efficient stripping. A low-cost, water-based mold master compound was developed as a replacement for traditional modeling clay, reducing material and labor costs by approximately 80 percent. The team also developed and tested unit sizes ranging from 50 pounds to a newly designed 7,000-pound unit intended for large-scale barrier reef, harbor protection, and military applications.

Field deployments at an established test site in Palm Bay, Florida demonstrated that Reef Arches units arranged in formation accumulate significant sediment behind them, creating conditions that support colonization by bottom-dwelling marine organisms. Coral growth was documented on deployed units at Summerland Key and through participation in the Plant a Million Corals restoration initiative. Independent academic research provided additional documentation of the technology’s ecological performance. The project received the Association of General Contractors Award for Innovative Technology and earned third-place recognition at the 2026 AGC Conference in Orlando, Florida, reflecting the technology’s commercial relevance across coastal engineering, habitat restoration, and infrastructure markets. This Phase I award has substantially reduced the technical and manufacturing risks associated with bringing Reef Arches to commercial scale and has positioned the company for Phase II development and market entry.
